stimulus.text: Historian Gordon Wood argues that Britain lost America largely because 'the British never found a way to translate battlefield victories into political control of a vast, hostile countryside.'

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE reason for the American victory in the Revolutionary War.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND reason for the American victory.
C. Briefly explain ONE advantage the British held in the war.
exemplar: France's entry into the war after Saratoga (1778) gave the Americans money, munitions, and — decisively — a navy that bottled up Cornwallis at Yorktown.
America's vast size worked against the British: with few cities and poor roads across a huge wilderness, British armies could win battles but never deliver a knockout blow.
Britain enjoyed the advantage of the world's most powerful navy, which blockaded American ports and moved troops freely along the coast.

stimulus.text:
"I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific... But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."
—Mark Twain, 1900 (abridged)

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of the United States asserting itself as a world power in the period 1890–1913.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of that assertion in the same period.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of Americans rejecting America's assertion as a world power.
exemplar: The United States asserted itself by annexing Hawaii in 1898 after American planters overthrew Queen Liliuokalani, extending American sovereignty into the Pacific.
Roosevelt's Corollary (1904) announced an American police power in the Caribbean, and the Panama Canal project (begun 1904) signaled American ambition for a two-ocean navy.
Americans rejected empire through the Anti-Imperialist League: figures like Mark Twain and Andrew Carnegie denounced the Philippine war as a betrayal of republican principles.

stimulus.attribution: Described from the map 'The Four Voyages of Christopher Columbus, 1492-1503.'
stimulus.text: The map shows the routes of Christopher Columbus's four voyages to the Americas, 1492-1503. The first voyage (1492-1493) sails from Spain to the Bahamas and the northern coast of Hispaniola. The second (1493-1496) reaches Dominica and explores the Caribbean islands. The third (1498-1500) sails farther south, touching the coast of present-day Venezuela in South America. The fourth (1502-1504) explores the coast of Central America. Outward and homeward tracks are numbered by voyage.

parts: A. Identify and briefly explain ONE pattern in European exploration shown by the routes on the map.
B. Briefly explain ONE way Columbus's voyages transformed life for Native Americans.
C. Briefly explain ONE way Columbus's voyages transformed life for Europeans.
exemplar: The map shows Columbus sailing steadily farther south and west with each voyage: the first lands in the Bahamas, while the third and fourth reach the South American mainland and Central America. The pattern reveals a deliberate, crown-sponsored program of exploration pushing deeper into unknown territory rather than a single accidental landfall.

For Native Americans the voyages were catastrophic. European diseases such as smallpox, to which Native peoples had no immunity, ravaged populations across the Caribbean and the mainland. The Spanish also imposed the encomienda system, forcing Native peoples into plantation labor and wiping out communities that resisted.

For Europeans the voyages opened access to the wealth of a new hemisphere. Silver and gold from Central and South America flowed to Spain, and new crops — potatoes, maize, tobacco — entered European diets and agriculture. The voyages also launched the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals, diseases, and ideas that permanently altered both continents.
